items.title: LabelLoop
items.where: X Square Robot Embodied Agent Hackathon · Scan and Sort Parcels · dual-arm robot · 2026
items.summary: A perception and control harness around a robot foundation model: it reads the shipping label, routes the parcel by rule, checks every grasp on camera and gives the model one sentence at a time.

facts.v: real-robot trials: 16,441 control cycles and 8,294 model calls, every one logged
on each of the four event scenarios, run on the real dual-arm robot
simulated episodes where the model alone lifted and placed the box, before the harness
camera frames saved across three cameras, so any run can be replayed
QR and barcode decoder, pincode OCR, and a phone held in the robot's claw as a scanner
to re-target the model after a person moves the parcel mid-task

deep: The gap: X Square's WALLX vision-language-action model turns one sentence into arm motion, but it cannot read a shipping label, pick a bin or confirm it really grasped the box. We built a simulation twin of the robot first and swept prompt strategies against the model alone: 17 simulated episodes, none lifted and placed the box. Better wording was never going to close that gap, so the loop was built around the model.

The relay: LabelLoop sits between the robot and the model. Every control cycle it takes three camera streams (head and two wrists) and both arms' joint states, runs perception, a step machine and a set of guards, and answers with an exact scripted motion, one short sentence for WALLX, or a hold. The same relay drives the Isaac Sim and X2Real twin and the real robot, so each behaviour was rehearsed before it touched hardware.

Perception: a zxing QR and barcode decoder with an upscale retry, a Tesseract pincode reader for small dense labels, and a phone held in the robot's own claw as a handheld scanner that streams frames to the relay. A parcel finder segments objects off the mat (never a bin or tray, with touching parcels split), a label finder locates the label, and a table-grid homography turns head-camera pixels into a 3 by 3 grid in metres. A pixel-to-arm-pose map is fitted from four recorded grasps.

Who moves: a step machine runs typed steps (replay a recorded motion, move, auto-pick, present the label, read, say a sentence, release, grip, hold the claw, wait for the parcel). The harness owns the exact motions: the pick, the flip, the in-air handover. WALLX owns open-ended placing, one sentence per call. The dashboard marks which of the two moved at every step, so the film never claims more of the model than it did.

Routing and verification: the ZIP prefix picks the bin by lookup (950, 951, 940, 941 to the blue lane and the left arm; 900, 901, 902 to the red lane and the right arm; anything else, or no readable label, to the black reject bin). A pick counts only when the claw closes on something and the parcel leaves its spot on camera. A drop counts only at the target with the claw open, and the parcel is confirmed in the bin on camera before the run is called done.

Live re-targeting: when a person moves the parcel, the harness sees it land in a new grid cell, cancels the old instruction, resets the model's history and re-targets within three control cycles. In the stress test, three moves produced three re-targets.

The debugging story: early real-robot runs kept ending the same way. Whatever the placing sentence, WALLX reached for a bin instead of the parcel. The fix was to hide what it must not touch: bins are painted out of the head image until the drop, only the target bin comes back for the place step, and a watchdog holds all motion if a bin region changes. A wording that tells the arms to squeeze the short ends then lifted a wide box clean off the table for the first real pick.

Guards and evidence: the idle arm is locked, the grip is latched while carrying, harness step names are never forwarded to the model, and one button stops and homes both arms. Every control cycle is logged with all three camera frames, the harness state and the exact sentence the model received. A replay dashboard animates the arms from the logs with inverse kinematics, and 269 tests keep the loop honest, including a full offline run against a stub model.

Where it stopped: asking WALLX to set a held box down inside a taped zone worked in some runs and not others (one series: 1 inside, 1 on the edge, 1 out), and asking it to pick with no destination never committed to a lift. Those moves stay scripted in the demo, and the replay says so.

decisions.b: Routing is a lookup on the ZIP prefix, never a model guess. No readable label, no bin: the parcel is flipped and rescanned, then rejected.
The model gets a single short, training-style sentence per call, or a hold. History is reset on every re-target so stale intent never leaks into the next move.

decisions.h: Hide what it must not touch
decisions.b: Bins are masked out of the head image until the drop. The model cannot grab what it cannot see, and a watchdog stops the run if a bin moves anyway.

decisions.h: One relay for sim and real
decisions.b: The same harness drives the Isaac Sim twin and the real robot, so every behaviour was rehearsed in simulation first.
Every cycle keeps all three camera frames, the harness state and the model's exact input. A failure is a replay, not a guess.
Harness motions and WALLX motions are labelled apart at every step, in the film and the dashboard.

items.owned: Team project. I owned the relay, the harness and step machine, label reading and parcel finding, calibration, the safety guards and the real-robot trials. My teammate built the replay dashboard and its arm kinematics, the table-grid homography and the scenario 4 WALLX work.

items.title: Sentinel AI
items.where: HP × SJSU Edge AI Hackathon · winner · 2026
items.summary: A fully local, privacy-first multi-camera safety system on the HP ZGX Nano: cheap on every frame, and expensive reasoning only when an escalation is credible. Video never leaves the machine.

facts.v: fps on a six-feed camera wall
frames agreed with the demo clip's labels
first synthesized audio on a warm voice connection

deep: Perception: YOLO26s-pose person and pose detection with temporal tracking; per-track motion rules (weapon, fall, run, loitering, sudden change) and optional CLIP screening keep the cheap path cheap.

Reasoning: a 16-frame evidence bundle goes to locally served Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B FP8 for event classification, WEAPON, FIGHT, THEFT, RUN, MEDICAL or BENIGN, plus a person description. Score-based escalation instead of every-frame VLM calls.

Operations: an incident state machine (NEW → ALERTED → DISPATCH_PENDING → DISPATCHED → TRACKING → RESOLVED / DISMISSED), SQLite event history, and a guarded emergency-call workflow with local speech recognition, ElevenLabs TTS, SignalWire telephony, human confirmation, a kill switch and one dispatch per incident.
Surface: a live multi-camera wall, site map, incident history, timeline, call transcript and operator actions over REST, WebSocket and MJPEG.

decisions.b: Cheap per-frame perception handles volume; the VLM handles the few ambiguous, high-impact events.
Video stays on the ZGX Nano, a privacy and latency choice, not a limitation.

items.title: Grounded SQL predicates
items.summary: Quality validation for ~409 active perception data miners: the LLM drafts a SQL true-positive predicate, the system executes and verifies it, and scoring is plain SQL over the full labeled population.

facts.v: failure discovery on miner state transitions

deep: Deterministic routing: miner → annotation task → task type → labeling view is a fixed mapping across classification, 2D detection, instance, track-attribute, sound-interval and 3D-cuboid tasks. A hallucinated view would produce a valid but wrong number, so routing never touches the LLM.

Grounding: the draft sees the miner description and selection config, the annotation ontology, valid label keys and the label vocabulary actually observed in the warehouse. Output: one scoped SQL boolean predicate.

Generate → execute → verify → retry: invalid SQL, unsupported fields, zero matches or vocabulary conflicts loop back into the next grounded attempt. The LLM only writes the rule; scoring never calls it.

Scoring stores precision, TP, denominator, labeled count, the lifecycle funnel, the labeling view and the canonical SQL. A new row is written only when TP or the denominator changes (~93% fewer writes).

Distribution: weekly Postgres aggregation into immutable versioned JSON snapshots plus an S3 manifest, read by a zero-backend Vite/TypeScript/Chart.js dashboard, a Slack digest and per-owner DMs. Failure alerts fire on the FAILED run-state transition.

decisions.b: Every number ships with the SQL that reproduces it; stored precision is a lower bound, and coverage gaps are audited.

items.title: SO-101 imitation learning
items.where: SJSU research · SO-101 + Hugging Face LeRobot
items.summary: Six-joint leader/follower arms with Feetech STS3215 servos: 50 teleoperated demonstrations, ACT trained from scratch on a ResNet-18 backbone and SmolVLA fine-tuning, then physical pick-and-place rollouts with video-measured error.

facts.v: physical pick-and-place trials at a fixed cube position

deep: Data: calibrated joint commands and synchronized RGB frames from paired cameras, with integrity validation, camera-dropout handling and resumable 50-trial rollout scripts.
Policies: ACT from scratch (30k and 60k step runs) and a fine-tuned SmolVLA (20k steps), both rolling out on the physical arm.

The debugging story: follower motor IDs reverted after power cycles and wrist-roll/gripper collided on one Feetech ID. Traced to an EEPROM write that was never re-locked, patched LeRobot's motor-bus setup to write Lock=1 after ID or baud changes, which persisted across restarts and unblocked calibration.
Evaluation: video-measured placement error, a failure taxonomy, and checkpoint-selection analysis across the two policy families.

decisions.b: Placement error is read off the camera, so the number is real.
ACT and the VLA are directly comparable because they share the demos.

items.title: AssistAI, wheelchair obstacle alert
items.where: SJSU, with Industrial & Systems Engineering and Audiology
items.summary: An AI obstacle-alert system for power wheelchairs where the real contribution is the human-machine interface: depth-triggered, multimodal warnings, twelve tactors plus speech or tone cues, measured by how fast a real person responds.

facts.v: confidence gate on YOLOv10n pedestrian detection
seatback tactor array in the published setup

deep: Perception: an onboard GPU laptop runs synchronized ZED 2i RGB and depth streams at 30 fps through pretrained YOLOv10n; box-center image-midline sets left/right, and a lightweight temporal association keeps one obstacle stable across frames to avoid duplicate warnings.
Trigger: box-center depth drives an inward crossing of roughly 1 m as the warning trigger; a pilot-measured ~1.65 s haptic actuation lag is compensated by movement speed × delay.
Warning design: instructional versus hazard-location content, speech versus non-speech cues, and seatback / wrist / no-vibration conditions, 12 warning designs in the expanded study.

Findings: seatback vibration was associated with stronger usefulness/satisfaction and, in the expanded study, shorter reaction times than audio-only; action-oriented warnings produced faster reactions and higher usefulness than informative/location-only; non-speech cues improved reaction time when tactile feedback was absent.

decisions.h: Measure the human, not just the model
decisions.b: Reaction time and preference are the real metrics of a useful warning.
A correct detection is not enough, the cue has to carry the decision to the driver fast.

papers.label: SAGE / HFES 2026, Communication strategy and vibrotactile feedback location
Elsevier / Transportation Research Part F, Vol. 123, 103801, Multimodal warning design

items.title: Transit Analytics
items.summary: A complete transit data platform: GTFS schedules and live departures meet in one Snowflake warehouse, and a forecasting layer sits on top, served through FastAPI and a React/TypeScript operator dashboard with text-to-SQL chat.

facts.v: AWS S3 + MWAA, and Azure Databricks/Delta

deep: Batch: gtfs_incremental lands BART and VTA GTFS every 6 h into a Snowflake LANDING schema.
Streaming: a Kafka producer polls the live departures API every 5 minutes; a consumer group writes events into the same LANDING zone, so static and live data share one place.
Modeling: dbt stages raw rows and joins trips, stops and routes per agency into analytics marts with route-level performance KPIs; an ml_forecast_dag trains on 90 days and forecasts 7 days ahead.
Serving: FastAPI serves KPIs, forecasts and a text-to-SQL chat; heavy ETL and training stay off the request path, and Snowflake and LLM keys live in AWS Secrets Manager.
Azure extension: on-time performance and service-reliability KPIs modeled in Azure Databricks with PySpark and Delta, ADF orchestration, SQL and Power BI with data-quality checks.

decisions.h: Stream and batch, one landing zone
decisions.b: Both paths land raw; dbt owns the cleanup.
Warehouse and LLM credentials in AWS Secrets Manager.

items.title: LSMStore, LSM-tree key-value store
items.summary: A Log-Structured Merge tree engine built from first principles: fsynced WAL, sorted memtables, immutable SSTables with Bloom filters, tombstones and crash-aware recovery.

facts.v: appended and fsynced before the memtable, replayed at startup
Bloom filters with seven hash functions on SSTables
trigger merges into one compacted table
startup replays the WAL and ignores a truncated final record

deep: Writes append to a write-ahead log and are fsynced before entering a sorted TreeMap memtable.
When the memtable fills, it flushes to an immutable sorted SSTable published through a temp file and an atomic rename.
Reads check the memtable, then newest-to-oldest SSTables using in-memory key-offset indexes and Bloom filters; deletes use tombstones.
A four-SSTable trigger merges tables in memory into one compacted table.

decisions.b: Atomic temp-file + rename publication makes every SSTable consistent, crash or no crash.

items.title: Blast Radius
items.summary: Answers the data-engineer's scariest question, 'if I rename this upstream field, what breaks before I merge?', with a fleet of coding agents and a human-controlled merge gate.

facts.v: downstream checks broken by one user_id → account_id rename
Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode working in own checkouts
coordinated fix PRs + tickets, all owner-approved
harmless optional-column case correctly reported as no-impact

deep: Trigger: an upstream PR posts to a Switch schema-changes room; an impact coordinator on Claude Code broadcasts an impact-checker role to linked analytics, ML-feature and dashboard rooms.
Bounded ownership: three agents work in their own Git checkouts, run the upstream branch against local tests, and report the exact failing file and check.
Repair: agents open Jira tickets and fix PRs, then wait for owner authorization, a non-owner's approval is rejected in the demo.
Gate: the coordinator writes a durable impact report and holds the upstream required check pending until every repo owner approves in Slack; the demo ends green only after legitimate owners sign off.

decisions.b: Each provider works in its own checkout; ownership and test scope are explicit.
The impact report stays pending until the humans approve, least privilege by construction.

items.title: CarbonShift
items.summary: GPU training that follows the grid: a 60-second control loop polls CAISO price and carbon, maps them to four Eco-Pulse states, and drives the A100's power cap through NVML, from full 250 W down to a checkpointed pause.

facts.v: lower carbon intensity in a realistic profile
WebSocket state updates to the dashboard

deep: Sensing: an async 60-second monitor polls CAISO OASIS (WattTime fallback) for $/MWh and gCO₂/kWh.
Decision: the Eco-Pulse engine maps thresholds over price and carbon to four states; GREEN raises the cap to 250 W, AMBER throttles to 150 W, RED saves a checkpoint, drops to 100 W and pauses.
Control: the GPU controller issues NVML power caps to the A100; the PyTorch training engine pause/resumes with a checkpoint manager, so a pause never loses progress.

Surface: FastAPI REST plus a WebSocket loop pushing state and running savings every 2 s to a React dashboard; a two-loop, two-clock design keeps the control loop (60 s) separate from the UI loop (2 s).

decisions.b: Power caps keep training moving; only RED stops it.
A red pause is free to resume, no progress lost.

items.title: SatCheck: will satellite internet work here?
items.where: Ready Builders Challenge · geospatial AI agent · 2026
items.summary: Will satellite internet actually work at this address? A Claude tool-use agent scores 4.67 million locations for tree-canopy and terrain obstruction, closing the gap between 'covered on the map' and 'works in practice'.

facts.v: of sites scored LOW obstruction risk

deep: Data chain: location coordinates and IDs join NLCD and USGS canopy rasters, USGS 3DEP elevation with derived slope, and NLCD land-cover classes; spatial sampling at each site feeds component scores into HIGH, MODERATE or LOW tiers using Starlink installation guidance.

Agent architecture: a Claude tool-use orchestrator decides the next step across five deterministic tools, ingest_locations, sample_environment, score_risk, validate_results, generate_report. Python does the geospatial and numeric work; file-based state passes artifact paths instead of millions of rows into the prompt.
Pipeline-only mode runs the same functions without an LLM; interactive tools analyze coordinates, addresses, areas, polygons and nearby alternatives over the precomputed scores.
Output: reports, charts and a scored CSV served through an interactive web app with a map and search.

decisions.b: The LLM orchestrates; the raster math is deterministic and testable.
Millions of rows never enter the prompt, only artifact paths do.

items.title: MarketMIX, MMM + MTA budget optimizer
items.summary: A unified marketing-measurement system: a Bayesian mix model and a survival multi-touch model over 16M journey events, joined by Shapley attribution and a constrained SLSQP optimizer that hands back a spendable budget plan.

facts.v: channel ROI error, vs 31% for last-touch
Criteo journey events in the survival model
attribution across channels, not one model's view

deep: Mix model: Bayesian MMM in PyMC Marketing with geometric adstock and Hill saturation; geo-lift experiment priors and transfer learning seed the coefficients.
Attribution: a discrete-time survival MTA over 16M Criteo journey events in PySpark, plus Shapley-value channel attribution.
Fusion: Shapley merges the mix model's incrementality with the survival model's path evidence into one set of channel contributions.
Optimization: constrained SciPy SLSQP budget optimization respects channel minimums and total spend, so the output is a plan, not coefficients. Prophet handles seasonality and promotions.

decisions.b: Attribution never hinges on a single model's view of the world.
The optimizer returns a spendable plan that respects minimums and total budget.

items.title: WikiRisk
items.summary: Predicts a harmful Wikipedia edit before it lands: historical Spark ingestion over 29+ GB of revisions trains a cross-validated model, then a live Structured Streaming job scores every event as it arrives.
deep: Training: Spark ingests 29+ GB of Wikipedia revisions and engineers author, diff and page features; SparkML models are cross-validated and tracked in MLflow over 11.16M rows.
Live: a Structured Streaming job consumes Wikimedia EventStreams and scores each edit as it lands; every scored event goes to a Parquet archive.
Serving: a SQLite serving store plus FastAPI health and search endpoints with tests keep the model queryable in production, not just a notebook.
Replay: the Parquet archive means any decision can be rebuilt and audited later.

decisions.b: The batch data teaches; the stream applies.
Scored events are durable, audit and replay for free.

items.title: AccessiMed
items.summary: A CLI-first accessibility scanner with reviewable fixes: Playwright + axe-core audits against WCAG 2.1 A/AA, deterministic or LLM remediation, and every change ships as a reviewed git diff into a CI gate.

facts.v: A/AA levels via axe-core in a real browser
fix strategies: deterministic no-key fallback + LLM
scan and remediation history, plus PDF reports
GitHub Actions gates keep it green

deep: Scan: install the CLI, initialize .accessimed.toml, then audit local HTML or run a real browser with Playwright and axe-core against WCAG 2.1 A/AA; findings normalize to severity and rule IDs (alt text, labels, button/link names, page language).
Fix: pick a finding and get a deterministic exact-match patch where one exists, or an LLM suggestion where it doesn't, detection is separated from remediation.
Review: apply the fix to source, review the git diff, re-run the checks; SQLite stores scans and remediation history and powers PDF reports and an optional FastAPI + React/Vite dashboard.
CI: GitHub Actions and automated test gates make accessibility a merge gate, not a one-time audit.

decisions.b: No-key fallbacks are fully predictable; the LLM only covers what rules can't.
Every change is a reviewed diff, a human is always in the loop.

items.title: Visual attention, measured
items.where: SJSU · Body Brain Connect · RSCA winner
items.summary: Whether eye and brain signals can objectively distinguish global, selective and sustained visual attention, built as a reproducible pipeline over Pupil Labs streams, and published in SAGE / HFES 2026.

facts.v: attention task types: global, selective, sustained
university competition winner, then CSU delegate

deep: Pipeline: Pupil Labs Core streams (gaze, fixation, blink, pupil, timing) per trial, with invalid-sample handling, temporal alignment, signal smoothing and feature extraction into fixation, blink, pupil and timing measures.
Validation: statistical comparison across the three task types identified which oculometric features best separate them, fixation count was the most sensitive in the pilot.
Output: gaze heatmaps, attention trajectories, model-ready features, and presentation-ready reports for HCI, human-factors and audiology audiences.
Why it matters: objective attention measures are the substrate for attention-aware interfaces, adaptive UIs and assistive systems.

decisions.b: Signals beat self-report when studying attention.
Clean → align → extract, as a repeatable pipeline, not a notebook.

papers.label: SAGE / HFES 2026, Measuring visual attention across concurrent and sequential tasks

items.title: Columnar query engine
items.summary: A mini analytical engine with an explicit plan, optimizer passes and a vectorized executor over column files with min/max skipping, checked against a row-at-a-time reference on 4M rows.

facts.v: randomized queries checked against a reference interpreter
row vectorized batches with selection vectors
row groups skipped by min/max on a one-year filter

deep: Plan: explicit logical operators, Scan, Filter, Project, Aggregate, HashJoin, Limit.
Optimizer: constant folding, filter pushdown through projections and joins into scans, and unused-column pruning.
Execution: batch-at-a-time vectorized execution over column vectors with selection vectors.
Storage: row-group columnar files with dictionary encoding, footer metadata and per-column min/max stats so predicates skip row groups before deserialization.

decisions.b: Randomized queries compared row-at-a-time keep the optimizer honest.

items.title: Order-book matching engine
items.summary: A single-instrument limit order book with O(1) cancels, correct reprice semantics and sub-microsecond tail latency on a multi-million-message replay.

facts.v: cancel via an order-ID hash index
randomized ops checked against a reference

deep: Structure: int64 tick prices, sorted price maps per side, FIFO queues per level, and an order-ID hash index of iterators for O(1) cancels.
Matching: marketable and IOC orders match by best price then time; size increases and reprices lose queue position, size reductions keep it.

decisions.b: 20k randomized operations checked against a reference before the latency numbers.

items.title: Dedup store
items.summary: FastCDC-style chunking with SHA-256 fingerprints and crash-resumable mark-and-sweep GC, plus replication that only sends what the far end is missing.

facts.v: journaled GC survives a crash mid-compaction

deep: Ingestion: parallel segmentation and hashing feed a bounded commit path of append-only containers with reference tracking.
GC: journaled mark-and-sweep compacts containers and resumes after a crash.
Replication: a simulated WAN sends only the chunks the peer lacks.

decisions.b: Compaction is durable, a crash mid-sweep resumes instead of corrupting.

items.title: CapFlow, CDC replication
items.where: SQL Server-style change data capture · Python
items.summary: A CDC pipeline that mirrors inserts, updates and deletes from a change log into warehouse tables, reconciles row by row, and can backfill or replay from a saved LSN.
deep: Capture: reads inserts, updates and deletes from the change log and advances commit-LSN cursors.
Apply: mirrors changes into warehouse tables with per-table lag reporting.
Verify: reconciles source and target row by row; supports backfill and replay from a saved LSN.

decisions.b: Every mirror is verified against the source row by row.

items.title: APM trace explorer
items.summary: Ingests OTLP/HTTP traces, assembles span trees and computes per-service and per-endpoint RED metrics with histogram percentiles, with a D3 service map, latency heatmap and rolling-baseline anomaly flags.

facts.v: HTTP trace ingestion into span trees
per-service and per-endpoint rates, errors, duration

deep: Ingest: OTLP/HTTP traces assembled into span trees with optional Redis and Postgres backends.
Analysis: RED metrics and histogram percentiles per service and endpoint; deploy-window comparison and rolling-baseline anomaly flags.
Tools: MCP-style incident tools (find_slow_endpoints, get_trace) built on the same store.

decisions.b: A ten-service e-commerce trace set with payment and inventory faults exercises the anomaly path.

items.title: GPU job orchestrator
items.summary: A scheduler API and Python SDK over 512 GPUs across AWS, GCP and on-prem pools: gang scheduling, tenant quotas, spot-preemption rollback and pool placement by cost and type.

facts.v: GPUs across AWS, GCP and on-prem pools
tail latency on the hot path

deep: Queue: jobs with idempotency keys enter a priority + FIFO queue, pass tenant quota checks, and filter pools by GPU type, cost and spot availability.
Placement: all-or-nothing gang scheduling with best-fit; jobs advance checkpoints and roll back to the last checkpoint on spot preemption, rescheduling on another pool.
Observability: health, job and pool APIs with Prometheus metrics.

decisions.b: Preemption rolls back to the last checkpoint instead of losing the job.

items.title: Agent fleet
items.summary: A CLI and dashboard that gives each coding-agent task its own Git branch and worktree, shards tests across workers, and gates every diff through a review gate before a human approves.

facts.v: each task runs isolated in Docker or a subprocess sandbox
deleted tests, weak assertions, secrets, network calls, large changes

deep: Isolation: each task gets its own branch and worktree, running in a Docker or subprocess sandbox.
Verification: test suites are sharded across workers using historical-duration LPT scheduling, and JUnit results are merged.
Review gate: a diff-review gate checks for deleted tests, weak assertions, secrets, network calls and large changes, with optional LLM review, then a human approves, retries or discards.

decisions.b: Agents can propose anything; only gated, reviewed diffs move.

items.title: Zoox, perception data platform
items.where: Zoox · Software Engineer Intern, Perception · May–Aug 2026
items.summary: The umbrella for the Zoox perception work: automated quality validation across ~409 data miners, weekly fleet snapshots, and a read-only ops Q&A, the single source for the company's story.

facts.v: PRs merged in small deployable slices

deep: See the pieces: Grounded SQL predicates (validation), Fleet reporting (snapshots and the tripwire), and the read-only ops bot, each has its own page with the full technical depth.
The through-line: LLM proposes, deterministic systems verify, production executes, and humans can reproduce every number.

decisions.b: The ops bot answers from published snapshots and holds zero execution tools.

items.title: Fleet reporting + failure tripwire
items.summary: Weekly Postgres snapshots of the whole miner fleet into immutable, versioned S3 artifacts, with event-driven failure alerts that cut discovery from days to minutes.

facts.v: failure discovery via the FAILED run-state transition

deep: Snapshots: Postgres aggregation into immutable versioned JSON plus an S3 manifest, read by a zero-backend dashboard.
Alerts: fire on the miner run-state transition to FAILED, event-driven, opt-in per miner; the owner gets miner identity, run ID, state, timestamp and a deep link.
Q&A: a read-only Slack bot answers from published snapshots, no tools, fenced untrusted context, bounded lengths, Vault-managed credentials.

decisions.b: The state machine is the source of truth; no polling for failures.

items.title: Read-only ops bot
items.summary: A Slack Q&A that can explain the fleet and never act on it: answers only from the published weekly snapshot, with both report and question fenced as untrusted data.

facts.v: the model holds no execution handle
report and question treated as untrusted context

deep: Prompt-injection defense by construction: an injected 'rerun all jobs' has nothing to call.
Ephemeral responses keep operational queries out of shared channels; failures reach owners as DMs.

decisions.b: The safest guardrail is a model that structurally can't do the thing.

items.title: TransitRisk, delay forecasting
items.summary: Predicts whether a station-route pair will see elevated delay in the next hour: seven classifiers, probability calibration, conformal prediction and a cost-optimal alert threshold when a miss costs 5× a false alarm.
deep: Models: naive Bayes, logistic regression, kNN, decision tree, random forest, SVM and XGBoost, with probability calibration and conformal prediction.
Decision theory: the alert threshold is chosen for cost, not accuracy, a missed delay costs five times a false alarm.
Surface: a Streamlit dashboard with per-route gauges, what-if controls, SHAP explanations and live-feed replay. 15 tests cover features, leakage, conformal coverage and targets.

decisions.b: Accuracy is the floor; the operating point is a business decision.

items.title: Warehouse case perception
items.summary: Detects cases in RGB-D warehouse frames and tracks them in 3D: YOLO/OpenCV detection, Kalman prediction, two-stage Hungarian assignment through occlusion, and depth back-projection to XYZ.

facts.v: tracks from RGB + depth, via pinhole back-projection

deep: Detection: Ultralytics YOLO or OpenCV on RGB; depth lookup and pinhole back-projection give XYZ.
Tracking: Kalman prediction plus two-stage Hungarian assignment keeps tracks alive through occlusion; collision-zone checks flag risky states.
Robustness: illumination, blur and occlusion variants, plus checkerboard and extrinsic calibration; C++ NMS keeps detection fast.

decisions.b: Cheap matching first, Hungarian only where it matters, robust to occlusion.

items.title: Real-time obstacle alert policy
items.summary: A hardware-independent wheelchair obstacle-alert prototype: multithreaded camera/LiDAR fusion mapping boxes to bearings, and a distance-triggered STOP/CAUTION policy with hysteresis and confirming frames.

facts.v: p95 capture-to-decision latency in the laptop simulator

deep: Latest-value slots: a frame slot and a scan slot drop stale work instead of queueing it, perception can never outrun the policy.
Fusion: a detector thread and a fusion+alert thread map camera boxes onto LiDAR bearings, so a 'person' is a thing in space, not a pixel.

Policy: depth drives the trigger, STOP under 1.0 m, CAUTION under 2.0 m, with a 0.25 m hysteresis band, two confirming frames to escalate and five to de-escalate, and immediate STOP for very close obstacles.

The shipped repo is a hardware-independent simulator with scripted detector and LiDAR streams plus interfaces for Jetson YOLOv8/TensorRT and ROS 2 integration, the published ZED 2i/YOLOv10n study lives on the wheelchair project page.

decisions.b: Latest-value slots mean a slow detector can't feed the policy stale geometry.

decisions.h: Distance, not detection, is the trigger
decisions.b: A box is a hint; the inward depth crossing is the cue, with hysteresis so it can't flicker.

items.title: Release pipelines that refuse bad changes
items.summary: Git-based delivery with automated schema checks and SQL test gates: Docker-standardized environments, CI that blocks schema drift before deploy, and the release-cycle speed that comes with it.

facts.v: commit → build → schema → SQL tests → deploy
schema checks and SQL tests as CI gates (Zscaler)
'works on my machine' classes of failure

deep: Coditas: backend services Dockerized with GitLab CI pipelines; automated build and deploy steps removed the manual release effort and kept staging and production parity.
Zscaler: Git-based workflows with automated schema checks and SQL tests in GitHub Actions; Docker standardized the build environment end to end.
The pipeline shape: on the first run, the schema check catches drift and blocks the change; on the next run every stage gets a green check and it deploys.

decisions.b: Schema and SQL tests gate each change, so drift never reaches production to be discovered.

items.title: Compiling Salesforce formulas into verified dbt SQL
items.summary: A metadata-driven compiler: pull formula definitions from the ObjectDetails API, walk the dependency graph depth-first, feed structured context to an LLM, and land validated SQL in version-controlled dbt models.

facts.v: lower reporting latency after incremental redesign
rows reconciled against the live CRM

deep: Pull: formula definitions and complete logic via the Salesforce ObjectDetails API.
Compile: depth-first traversal maps every nested dependency into a structured JSON context per formula field.
Generate: the LLM emits optimized SQL from that structured context; the transforms are inserted into dbt models for warehouse execution.
Verify: automated sampling compares transformed output against live CRM, flags discrepancies programmatically, and reconciliation dashboards gate deployment.
Ingestion: incremental upserts with change detection, modular transformation layering, and partitioning/clustering tuned for Snowflake; secrets in AWS Secrets Manager.

decisions.b: Prompt tuning alone is not a control; sampled reconciliation against source truth is.

decisions.h: Deterministic SQL out of a dynamic source
decisions.b: The formula logic is compiled once into versioned, reproducible warehouse code.

items.title: An 800 TB HDFS → S3 migration behind a test gate
items.summary: Controlled enterprise migration: AWS Data Sync moves the bytes, bash tracks every batch, and a Delta Lake + pytest validation framework proves source and destination match before go-live.

facts.v: migrated with zero production data errors
one major reporting pipeline, after CTE + partition rewrites

deep: Transfer: AWS Data Sync with bash scripts copying and tracking every batch.
Validation: Delta Lake–style change tracking plus Python/pytest dataset checks comparing source and destination for row mismatches, null anomalies and type drift, flagged before release.
SLAs: CloudWatch metrics, SNS alerts and Lambda triggers orchestrated in Airflow detect SLA breaches and log root-cause traces; containerized, modular MWAA-style DAGs replaced the legacy pipelines.
Performance: layered CTE structure, partition pruning and execution tuning took a major reporting model from ~18 to 6 minutes.

decisions.b: Validation gates make the move auditable, a small failure can't cascade into a client reporting error.

items.summary: Rare-event retrieval for AV data: rule filters, embedding search, Rocchio feedback and a hybrid re-ranker compared at a fixed 300-result review budget over an IVF index.

items.title: AV trajectory prediction

items.summary: A CPU roofline and kernel harness: dot product, STREAM triad and SGEMM in scalar, SIMD, reordered and cache-blocked variants. SGEMM climbs 1.27 → 36.11 GFLOP/s.

items.title: AI CodeGate
items.where: Merge gate with an audit trail
items.summary: A merge gate that combines deterministic diff, lint and unit-test checks with a severity-rated LLM reviewer. A change lands only if every hard check passes, and every decision is appended to a hash-chained audit log.

items.title: Case Automation Agent
items.summary: Triage, planning and execution as separate layers. One executor enforces approval and permission checks before any tool call, for both the deterministic planner and the Claude planner, with an append-only audit.

items.title: Rx Fulfillment API
items.summary: Telehealth orders that survive retries: idempotent payment and pharmacy webhooks, a transactional outbox, an audit log and field-level encryption on a tRPC and Drizzle order state machine.

items.title: Multiplayer Agent Sessions
items.where: SJSU team project · humans and agents in one session
items.summary: A shared workspace where people and AI agents edit the same session with handoff, concurrency, interruption and rollback. I own the session service, model serving, infrastructure and CI.

facts.v: model tasks: catch-up, intent, merge, routing
versioned SessionEvent schema for every action
OpenAPI serving boundary for the TypeScript client

deep: Every human or agent action is a versioned SessionEvent in an append-only log, so interruption, handoff and rollback are just events.

Four model tasks: M1 catch-up summarization when someone joins, M2 intent attribution, M3 merge and arbitration between conflicting edits, M4 decomposition and routing of work, compared against a MAST baseline.

I own the session service, model serving on /v1/models/{model_id}/predict behind an OpenAPI boundary, shared model code, the M1 catch-up model, Docker infrastructure, CI workflows, evaluation configs and the ADRs.

items.title: IoT Smart Garden
items.where: Edge to cloud · ESP32 and Azure
items.summary: Soil moisture, temperature and humidity from ESP32 sensors stream over MQTT into Azure IoT Hub and Azure SQL. Python checks catch faulty sensors, Power Automate raises alerts and Power BI tracks device health, replacing a manual watering schedule.

facts.v: into Azure IoT Hub and Azure SQL

deep: ESP32 boards publish soil moisture, temperature and humidity over MQTT to Azure IoT Hub, landing in Azure SQL.
Python validation flags sensor faults (stuck, out-of-range or missing readings) before they reach decisions.
Power Automate sends alerts and Power BI reports device and usage health, so watering follows the soil instead of a calendar.

items.title: SDLC Context Graph
items.summary: Pull requests, reviews, CI runs, deploys, tickets and incidents from 40 repositories in one property graph, plus a tool-using agent that answers root-cause questions with cited evidence.

facts.v: ground-truth questions in the eval set
agent tools: graph, metrics, vector search

deep: A SQLite property graph links teams, people, services, commits, PRs, CI outcomes, deploys and incidents.
DORA-style weekly metrics and a hashed TF-IDF vector index over PR and incident text.
The agent calls graph_query, metric_lookup and vector_search and must cite the evidence it used; it is scored on 148 ground-truth questions.

items.title: Campaign and Retention Agents
items.summary: From a marketing goal to audience, content and a scheduled send, with consent, unsubscribe and frequency checks enforced in one executor. A Thompson-sampling bandit picks the message variant and send hour from conversion feedback.

facts.v: sampling bandit for variant and send hour

deep: Audience selection, brand and product retrieval, and content generation feed a central executor that checks consent, unsubscribe status and send frequency.
An async job queue with retries and idempotency keys runs scheduled sends; every action lands in an audit ledger.
A Thompson-sampling contextual bandit learns which variant and send hour convert.

items.title: LakeLog
items.summary: The core of Delta Lake and Iceberg style tables, built from scratch: an ordered log of versioned commits, optimistic concurrent writers where exactly one wins each version, snapshots, time travel and data skipping.

facts.v: per version via atomic filesystem link

deep: Immutable partitioned data files and an ordered _log of versioned commits.
Optimistic writers publish with an atomic link so exactly one wins a version; non-conflicting appends retry automatically.
Checkpoints every ten versions, min/max file stats for data skipping, copy-on-write deletes, small-file compaction and retention-aware vacuum.

items.title: pg-wal-lab
items.summary: A PostgreSQL C extension for inspecting the write-ahead log and MVCC row versions, plus a crash-recovery harness, built with PGXS against PostgreSQL 14 to 16 in CI.

facts.v: built and tested in GitHub Actions

items.title: Edge LLM Roofline
items.where: ML systems · LLM inference on edge chips
items.summary: An analytical model that predicts LLM prefill and decode speed, memory bandwidth and KV-cache size on edge NPUs. It matched real Jetson Orin and RTX 4090 measurements within 8.7% error.

facts.v: MAPE vs measured Jetson Orin and RTX 4090
more tokens/s from doubling bandwidth vs compute

deep: Computes layer FLOPs, weight and KV bytes, SRAM-limited re-reads and the roofline bound for Llama 3.2 1B/3B and Phi-3 Mini at FP16, INT8 and INT4.
Separates prefill (tiled GEMM and attention) from decode (weight streaming, GEMV, KV traffic).
Validated against Nsight Compute, PyTorch Profiler and llama.cpp measurements; the sweep shows decode is bandwidth-bound beyond 4 MB of SRAM.

items.title: GPU Performance and Attention Lab
items.summary: Benchmarks and fused attention on an RTX 5090: fused attention cut peak memory from 16,648 MiB to 264 MiB at 16k tokens and latency from 46.8 ms to 27.1 ms.

facts.v: less peak memory with fused attention

facts.v: draft lengths compared to a baseline

items.summary: Plans how to split dense and mixture-of-experts LLMs across devices: tensor, expert and pipeline parallel degrees ranked by prefill latency and decode throughput, with a torch.distributed correctness check.

items.summary: Lowers a GPT-2 block from torch.fx into a typed SSA dataflow IR, fuses operators, and places fused stages on a 2D processing-element grid with SRAM-fitting tiles to estimate cycles and memory traffic.

items.title: Fleet Control Plane
items.summary: A Go service for camera and sensor fleets: versioned desired versus reported config shadows, conditional writes that reject stale versions, heartbeat liveness and retried asynchronous config push.

items.title: Sensor Hub Firmware
items.summary: No-heap IMU hub firmware core: 1 kHz sensor reads, fixed-point complementary filter, a lock-free ISR ring buffer, CRC-framed messaging, watchdog fault handling and A/B firmware updates with rollback, on a fault-injectable hardware layer.
